blocks.tex: \textbf{5} Prove, from first principles, that the derivative of $6x$ is 6.

parts.text: both mean the gradient function, also known as the derivative of

blocks.tex: $\mathrm f(x)=6x$.\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathrm f(x+h)-\mathrm f(x)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{6(x+h)-6x}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{6x+6h-6x}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{6h}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}6.\end{aligned}\]So $\mathrm f'(x)=6$.
\textbf{6} Prove, from first principles, that the derivative of $4x^2$ is $8x$.

parts.text: both mean the gradient function, also known as the derivative of

blocks.tex: $\mathrm f(x)=4x^2$.\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathrm f(x+h)-\mathrm f(x)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4(x+h)^2-4x^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4x^2+8xh+4h^2-4x^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{8xh+4h^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{h(8x+4h)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}(8x+4h).\end{aligned}\]As $h\to0$, $8x+4h\to8x$. So $\mathrm f'(x)=8x$.

blocks.tex: $\mathrm f(z)=az^2$.\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm f'(z)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathrm f(z+h)-\mathrm f(z)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{a(z+h)^2-az^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{az^2+2azh+ah^2-az^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{2azh+ah^2}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{h(2az+ah)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}(2az+ah).\end{aligned}\]As $h\to0$, $2az+ah\to2az$. So $\mathrm f'(z)=2az$.

\textbf{Challenge}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=\frac1x$.
\textbf{a} Given that $\mathrm f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathrm f(x+h)-\mathrm f(x)}h$, show that $\mathrm f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-1}{x^2+xh}$.
\textbf{b} Deduce that $\mathrm f'(x)=-\frac1{x^2}$.

\textbf{a}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=\frac1x$.\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathrm f(x+h)-\mathrm f(x)}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac1{x+h}-\frac1x}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac{x-(x+h)}{x(x+h)}}h\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-h}{xh(x+h)}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-1}{x(x+h)}\\&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-1}{x^2+hx}.\end{aligned}\]
\textbf{b} As $h\to0$, $\dfrac{-1}{x^2+hx}\to-\dfrac1{x^2}$. So $\mathrm f'(x)=-\dfrac1{x^2}$.

blocks.tex: \textbf{5} Find the gradients of the curve $y=x^2-5x+10$ at the points $A$ and $B$ where the curve meets the line $y=4$.

The curve $y=x^2-5x+10$ meets the line $y=4$ when: $x^2-5x+10=4$, $x^2-5x+6=0$, $(x-3)(x-2)=0$, $x=3$ or $x=2$.
Gradient of curve $=\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2x-5$.
When $x=3$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2\times3-5=1$.
When $x=2$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2\times2-5=-1$.
So the gradient is $-1$ at $(2,4)$ and 1 at $(3,4)$.
\textbf{6} Find the gradients of the curve $y=2x^2$ at the points $C$ and $D$ where the curve meets the line $y=x+3$.

The curve $y=2x^2$ meets the line $y=x+3$ when $2x^2=x+3$, $2x^2-x-3=0$, $(2x-3)(x+1)=0$, $x=1.5$ or $-1$.
Gradient of curve $=\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4x$.
When $x=-1$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4\times-1=-4$.
When $x=1.5$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4\times1.5=6$.
So the gradient is $-4$ at $(-1,2)$ and 6 at $(1.5,4.5)$.

\textbf{7}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=x^2-2x-8$.
\textbf{a} Sketch the graph of $y=\mathrm f(x)$.
\textbf{b} On the same set of axes, sketch the graph of $y=\mathrm f'(x)$.
\textbf{c} Explain why the $x$-coordinate of the turning point of $y=\mathrm f(x)$ is the same as the $x$-coordinate of the point where the graph of $y=\mathrm f'(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.

\textbf{a}\quad $y=\mathrm f(x)=x^2-2x-8$. As $a=1$ is positive, the graph has a $\cup$ shape and a minimum point.
When $x=0$, $y=-8$, so the graph crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,-8)$.
When $y=0$, $x^2-2x-8=0$, $(x+2)(x-4)=0$, $x=-2$ or $x=4$, so the graph crosses the $x$-axis at $(-2,0)$ and $(4,0)$.
Completing the square: $x^2-2x-8=(x-1)^2-1-8=(x-1)^2-9$.
So the minimum point has coordinates $(1,-9)$.

blocks.tex: \textbf{6}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=\frac{12}{p\sqrt x}+x$, where $p$ is a real constant and $x>0$. Given that $\mathrm f'(2)=3$, find $p$, giving your answer in the form $a\sqrt2$ where $a$ is a rational number.

$\mathrm f(x)=\frac{12}{p\sqrt x}+x=\frac{12}p x^{-1/2}+x$, $\mathrm f'(2)=3$.
$\mathrm f'(x)=-\frac12\times\frac{12}p x^{-1/2-1}+1=-\frac6p x^{-3/2}+1$.

$\mathrm f'(2)=-\frac6p(2)^{-3/2}+1=-\frac6{2p\sqrt2}+1$.
$-\frac6{2p\sqrt2}+1=3$, $-\frac6{2p\sqrt2}=2$.
$p=-\frac3{2\sqrt2}=-\frac3{2\sqrt2}\times\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=-\frac34\sqrt2$.

\textbf{7}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=(2-x)^9$.
\textbf{a} Find the first 3 terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $\mathrm f(x)$, giving each term in its simplest form.
\textbf{b} If $x$ is small, so that $x^2$ and higher powers can be ignored, show that $\mathrm f'(x)\approx9216x-2304$.

\textbf{a}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=(2-x)^9=2^9+\binom91 2^8(-x)+\binom92 2^7(-x)^2+\cdots=512-2304x+4608x^2$.
\textbf{b}\quad $\mathrm f(x)\approx512-2304x+4608x^2$.
$\mathrm f'(x)\approx-2304+2\times4608x^{2-1}=9216x-2304$.

blocks.tex: \textbf{3} Find the coordinates of the point where the tangent to the curve $y=x^2+1$ at the point $(2,5)$ meets the normal to the same curve at the point $(1,2)$.

$y=x^2+1$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2x$. When $x=2$ and $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4$. So the equation of the tangent at $(2,5)$ is $y-5=4(x-2)$, $y=4x-3$.
When $x=1$, gradient of curve $=2$. So gradient of normal is $-\frac12$. The equation of the normal is $y-2=-\frac12(x-1)$, $y=-\frac12x+2\frac12$.

Tangent at $(2,5)$ and normal at $(1,2)$ meet when $4x-3=-\frac12x+2\frac12$, $8x-6=-x+5$, $9x=11$, $x=\frac{11}9$.
$y=4\times\frac{11}9-3=\frac{17}9$.
So the tangent at $(2,5)$ meets the normal at $(1,2)$ at $\left(\frac{11}9,\frac{17}9\right)$.
\textbf{4} Find the equations of the normals to the curve $y=x+x^3$ at the points $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$, and find the coordinates of the point where these normals meet.

$y=x+x^3$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=1+3x^2$. When $x=0$, gradient of curve $=1+3\times0^2=1$. So gradient of normal is $-\frac11=-1$.
The equation of the normal at $(0,0)$ is $y-0=-1(x-0)$, $y=-x$.
When $x=1$, gradient of curve $=1+3\times1^2=4$. So gradient of normal is $-\frac14$.

The equation of the normal at $(1,2)$ is $y-2=-\frac14(x-1)$, $4y-8=-x+1$, $4y+x-9=0$.
Normals at $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$ meet when $4(-x)+x-9=0$, $3x=-9$, $x=-3$, $y=3$. The normals meet at $(-3,3)$.
\textbf{5} For $\mathrm f(x)=12-4x+2x^2$, find the equations of the tangent and the normal at the point where $x=-1$ on the curve with equation $y=\mathrm f(x)$.

$y=\mathrm f(x)=12-4x+2x^2$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=0-4+4x=4x-1$.
When $x=-1$, $y=12-4(-1)+2(-1)^2=18$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4(-1)-4=-8$.
The tangent at $(-1,18)$ has gradient $-8$. So its equation is $y-18=-8(x+1)$, $y-18=-8x-8$, $y=-8x+10$.
The normal at $(-1,18)$ has gradient $\frac{-1}{-8}=\frac18$. So its equation is $y-18=\frac18(x+1)$, $8y-144=x+1$, $8y-x-145=0$.

\textbf{6} The point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $\frac12$ lies on the curve with equation $y=2x^2$. The normal to the curve at $P$ intersects the curve at points $P$ and $Q$. Find the coordinates of $Q$. (6 marks)

$y=2x^2$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4x$.
When $x=\frac12$, $y=2\times(\frac12)^2=\frac12$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4\times\frac12=2$.
So gradient of normal is $-\frac12$. The equation of the normal at $(\frac12,\frac12)$ is $y-\frac12=-\frac12(x-\frac12)$, $y=-\frac12x+\frac34$.

The normal intersects the curve when $2x^2=-\frac12x+\frac34$, $8x^2+2x-3=0$, $(4x+3)(2x-1)=0$, $x=-\frac34$ or $\frac12$.
$x=\frac12$ is point $P$, so $x=-\frac34$ must be point $Q$.
When $x=-\frac34$, $y=-\frac12(-\frac34)+\frac34=\frac98$. Point $Q$ is $(-\frac34,\frac98)$.

blocks.tex: \textbf{3} Show that the function $\mathrm f(x)=4-x(2x^2+3)$ is decreasing for all $x\in\mathbb R$.

$\mathrm f(x)=4-x(2x^2+3)=4-2x^3-3x$, $\mathrm f'(x)=-6x^2-3$.
$x^2\ge0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$, so $-6x^2-3\le0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
Therefore, $\mathrm f(x)$ is decreasing for all $x\in\mathbb R$.

\textbf{4 a} Given that the function $\mathrm f(x)=x^2+px$ is increasing on the interval $[-1,1]$, find one possible value for $p$.
\textbf{b} State with justification whether this is the only possible value for $p$.

\textbf{a}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=x^2+px$, $\mathrm f'(x)=2x+p\ge0$ when $-1\le x\le1$.
When $x=-1$, $\mathrm f'(x)=-2+p\ge0$, so $p\ge2$. So for $\mathrm f'(x)\ge0$, $p\ge2$, e.g. $p=3$.
When $x=1$, $\mathrm f'(x)=2+p\ge0$, so $p\ge-2$. However, $p\ge2$ to work with $x=-1$.
\textbf{b} Using the proof from part \textbf{a}, any value $p\ge2$ will work.

blocks.tex: \textbf{5} By considering the gradient on either side of the stationary point on the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x$, show that this point is a point of inflection. Sketch the curve $y=x^3-3x^2+3x$.

$y=x^3-3x^2+3x$, $\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3x^2-6x+3$.
Putting $3x^2-6x+3=0$, $3(x^2-2x+1)=0$, $3(x-1)^2=0$, $x=1$.
When $x=1$, $y=1$. So $(1,1)$ is a stationary point.
Considering points near to $(1,1)$:
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0.9&1&1.1\\\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}&0.03&0&0.03\\&+\mathrm{ve}&0&+\mathrm{ve}\\\text{Shape}&/&-&/\end{array}$
The gradient on either side of $(1,1)$ is positive, so $(1,1)$ is a point of inflection.
\textbf{6} Find the maximum value and hence the range of values for the function $\mathrm f(x)=27-2x^4$.

$\mathrm f(x)=27-2x^4$, $\mathrm f'(x)=-8x^3$. Putting $-8x^3=0$, $x=0$. When $x=0$, $y=27$. So $(0,27)$ is a stationary point.
$\mathrm f''(x)=-24x^2$. When $x=0$, $\mathrm f''(x)=0$, so not conclusive.
Considering points near to $(0,27)$:
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&-0.1&0&0.1\\\mathrm f'(x)&0.008&0&-0.008\\&+\mathrm{ve}&0&-\mathrm{ve}\\\text{Shape}&/&-&/\end{array}$
So $(0,27)$ is a maximum point. So the maximum value of $\mathrm f(x)$ is 27 and the range of values is $\mathrm f(x)\le27$.

Consider $\mathrm f(x)=ax^3-6ax^2+(12a+12)x-(8a+16)$.
Since $\mathrm f(2)=8$ and $\mathrm f'(2)=12$, the curve $y=\mathrm f(x)$ touches $y=x^3$ at $(2,8)$: notice that both calculations are necessary to prove that the curves touch.
To find the other intersection point, let $\mathrm f(x)=x^3$.
$\Rightarrow(a-1)x^3-6ax^2+(12a+12)x-(8a+16)=0$.
Substituting $x=2$: $8(a-1)-24a+2(12a+12)-(8a+16)=0$.
$\Rightarrow(x-2)[(a-1)x^2-(4a+2)x+(4a+8)]=0$ (notice that factorising by inspection is much easier than using a method such as long division).
Substituting $x=2$ into the quadratic factor: $4(a-1)-2(4a+2)+(4a+8)=0$.
$\Rightarrow(x-2)(x-2)[(a-1)x-(2a+4)]=0$.
So the other intersection point has coordinates $\left(\frac{2a+4}{a-1},\left[\frac{2a+4}{a-1}\right]^3\right)$.
\textbf{(i)} When $a=2$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}=8$.
Hence the two graphs touch at $(2,8)$ and intersect at $(8,512)$.
$y=2x^3-12x^2+36x-32$ has no turning points: consider the derivative $6x^2-24x+36=0$.
\textbf{(ii)} When $a=1$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}$ is undefined.

$y=x^3-6x^2+24x-24$ has no turning points: consider the derivative $3x^2-12x+24=0$.
\textbf{(iii)} When $a=-2$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}=0$.
Hence the two graphs touch at $(2,8)$ and intersect at $(0,0)$.

\textbf{2}\quad $\mathrm f(x)=(x+1)(x-4)^2$.
\textbf{a} Sketch the graph of $y=\mathrm f(x)$.
\textbf{b} On a separate set of axes, sketch the graph of $y=\mathrm f'(x)$.
\textbf{c} Show that $\mathrm f'(x)=(x-4)(3x-2)$.
\textbf{d} Use the derivative to determine the exact coordinates of the points where the gradient function cuts the coordinate axes.

\textbf{a} $y=\mathrm f(x)=(x+1)(x-4)^2=x^3-7x^2+8x+16$.
When $y=0$, $x=-1$ or $x=4$.
To find stationary points, $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=0$:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}&=3x^2-14x+8\\
(3x-2)(x-4)&=0\\
x&=\frac23\text{ or }x=4.
\end{aligned}\]
When $x=\frac23$, $y=(\frac23+1)(\frac23-4)^2=\frac{500}{27}$.
When $x=4$, $y=(4+1)(4-4)^2=0$.
So $(\frac23,\frac{500}{27})$ and $(4,0)$ are stationary points.
\[\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=6x-14.\]
When $x=\frac23$, $\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=6(\frac23)-14=-10<0$.
So $(\frac23,\frac{500}{27})$ is a maximum.
When $x=4$, $\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=6(4)-14=10>0$.
So $(4,0)$ is a minimum.

\textbf{c} $\begin{aligned}\mathrm f(x)&=(x+1)(x-4)^2=x^3-7x^2+8x+16\\
\mathrm f'(x)&=3x^2-14x+8\\&=(3x-2)(x-4).\end{aligned}$

\textbf{d} $\mathrm f'(x)=3x^2-14x+8$

$(3x-2)(x-4)=0$

$x=\dfrac23$ or $x=4$

When $x=0$, $\mathrm f'(x)=8$.

The points where the gradient function cuts the axes are $(\frac23,0)$, $(4,0)$ and $(0,8)$.

\textbf{6} A rectangular garden is fenced on three sides, and the house forms the fourth side of the rectangle.

\textbf{a} Given that the total length of the fence is $80\,\mathrm m$, show that the area, $A$, of the garden is given by the formula $A=y(80-2y)$, where $y$ is the distance from the house to the end of the garden.

\textbf{b} Given that the area is a maximum for this length of fence, find the dimensions of the enclosed garden, and the area which is enclosed.

textRegions.tex:
Let the width of the garden be $x\,\mathrm m$.
Then $x+2y=80$
\[x=80-2y\qquad(1)\]
$\begin{aligned}\text{Area }A&=xy\\&=y(80-2y)\\&=80y-2y^2.\end{aligned}$

blocks.tex:
\textbf{b} $\dfrac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dy}=80-4y$.
Putting $\dfrac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dy}=0$ for maximum area:
\[80-4y=0\qquad y=20.\]
Substituting in (1): $x=40$.
So area $=40\,\mathrm m\times20\,\mathrm m=800\,\mathrm m^2$.

\textbf{7} A closed cylinder has total surface area equal to $600\pi$.
\textbf{a} Show that the volume, $V\,\mathrm{cm}^3$, of this cylinder is given by the formula $V=300\pi r-\pi r^3$, where $r\,\mathrm{cm}$ is the radius of the cylinder.
\textbf{b} Find the maximum volume of such a cylinder.

\textbf{a} Total surface area $=2\pi rh+2\pi r^2$.
\[\begin{aligned}2\pi rh+2\pi r^2&=600\pi\\rh&=300-r^2.\end{aligned}\]
Volume $=\pi r^2h=\pi r(rh)=\pi r(300-r^2)$.
So $V=300\pi r-\pi r^3$.

\textbf{b} For maximum volume, $\dfrac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dr}=0$.
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dV}{\mathrm dr}&=300\pi-3\pi r^2\\300\pi-3\pi r^2&=0\\r^2&=100\\r&=10.\end{aligned}\]
Substituting $r=10$ into $V$ gives:
\[V=300\pi\times10-\pi\times10^3=2000\pi.\]
Maximum volume $=2000\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^3$.

\textbf{9} A shape consists of a rectangular base with a semicircular top, as shown.

\textbf{a} Given that the perimeter of the shape is $40\,\mathrm{cm}$, show that its area, $A\,\mathrm{cm}^2$, is given by the formula
\[A=40r-2r^2-\frac{\pi r^2}2\]

where $r\,\mathrm{cm}$ is the radius of the semicircle. \hfill (2 marks)

\textbf{b} Hence find the maximum value for the area of the shape. \hfill (4 marks)

Let the rectangle have dimensions $2r$ by $x\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Perimeter of figure $=(2r+2x+\pi r)\,\mathrm{cm}$

Perimeter $=40\,\mathrm{cm}$, so
\[2r+2x+\pi r=40,\qquad x=\frac{40-\pi r-2r}2.\]
$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}&=\text{rectangle}+\text{semicircle}\\&=2rx+\frac12\pi r^2.\end{aligned}$

Substituting $x=\dfrac{40-\pi r-2r}2$:
\[\begin{aligned}A&=r(40-\pi r-2r)+\frac12\pi r^2\\&=40r-2r^2-\frac12\pi r^2.\end{aligned}\]

\textbf{b} For maximum area, $\dfrac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dr}=0$:
\[\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dr}=40-4r-\pi r,\qquad40-4r-\pi r=0.\]

$r=\dfrac{40}{4+\pi}$.
When $r=\frac{40}{4+\pi}$,
\[\begin{aligned}
A&=40\times\frac{40}{4+\pi}-2\left(\frac{40}{4+\pi}\right)^2-\frac12\pi\left(\frac{40}{4+\pi}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{1600}{4+\pi}-\left(2+\frac12\pi\right)\left(\frac{40}{4+\pi}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{1600}{4+\pi}-\frac{4+\pi}{2}\times\frac{1600}{(4+\pi)^2}\\
&=\frac{1600}{4+\pi}-\frac{800}{4+\pi}\\&=\frac{800}{4+\pi}.
\end{aligned}\]
So maximum area $=\dfrac{800}{4+\pi}\,\mathrm{cm}^2$.

\textbf{10} The shape shown is a wire frame in the form of a large rectangle split by parallel lengths of wire into 12 smaller equal-sized rectangles.

\textbf{a} Given that the total length of wire used to complete the whole frame is $1512\,\mathrm{mm}$, show that the area of the whole shape, $A\,\mathrm{mm}^2$, is given by the formula
\[A=1296x-\frac{108x^2}7\]

where $x\,\mathrm{mm}$ is the width of one of the smaller rectangles. \hfill (4 marks)

\textbf{b} Hence find the maximum area which can be enclosed in this way. \hfill (4 marks)

\textbf{a} Total length of wire $=(18x+14y)\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Length $=1512\,\mathrm{mm}$, so
\[18x+14y=1512,\qquad y=\frac{1512-18x}{14}.\]
Total area $A\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ is given by: $A=2y\times6x$.
Substituting $y=\frac{1512-18x}{14}$:
\[A=12x\left(\frac{1512-18x}{14}\right)=1296x-\frac{108}{7}x^2.\]

\textbf{b} For maximum area $\dfrac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dx}=0$:
\[\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dx}&=1296-\frac{216}{7}x\\1296-\frac{216}{7}x&=0\\x&=\frac{7\times1296}{216}=42.\end{aligned}\]
When $x=42$,
\[A=1296\times42-\frac{108}{7}\times42^2=27\,216.\]
Maximum area $=27\,216\,\mathrm{mm}^2$.
(Check: $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2A}{\mathrm dx^2}=-\dfrac{216}{7}<0\ \therefore\text{ maximum}$)

\[A=\frac{16a^2\pi}{2}+\frac{(4a-x)^2\pi}{4}+\frac{(2a-x)^2\pi}{4}+\frac{(2a+x)^2\pi}{4}+\frac{x^2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}(56a^2+4x^2-8ax).\]
